name: Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control
description: Learn the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control in BJJ. Complete guide covering grip transitions, finishing mechanics, and defensive counters.
target_area: Carotid arteries (compressed by opponent's own shoulder and your arm)
summary: The Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control is a head-and-arm blood choke that converts the opponent's own shoulder-frame defense into a trapped arm, compressing both carotids while leg entanglement and lateral torque keep their posture broken.
overview:
The Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control exploits the unique rotational mechanics and lateral torque inherent to this position, trapping the opponent's arm against their own neck to create bilateral carotid compression. Unlike standard arm triangles initiated from traditional side control, this variation leverages the leg entanglement and shoulder pressure of Twister Side Control to naturally disrupt the defender's postural alignment, making it significantly harder to create the frames and bridges that typically counter arm triangle attempts.

Strategically, this submission capitalizes on a specific and common defensive reaction. When the bottom player frames against shoulder pressure or attempts to turn into the top player to relieve spinal torque, their arm frequently crosses their own neck, establishing the trapped-arm configuration essential for the head-and-arm choke. Recognizing this frame defense as a submission trigger rather than a positional threat is the key tactical insight. The finish requires transitioning to a perpendicular angle and applying progressive chest-to-chest compression, using body mechanics rather than arm strength to generate the choking pressure.

The position integrates naturally into the Twister Side Control attack chain alongside darce chokes, kimuras, and the twister itself. When opponents defend the primary spinal attacks by creating frames, they inadvertently set up the arm triangle, creating a defensive dilemma where protecting against one threat opens vulnerability to another.

injury_risks.injury: Loss of consciousness from blood choke
injury_risks.recovery_time: Immediate recovery if released promptly; potential stroke risk if held too long

injury_risks.injury: Neck strain from improper pressure angle
Shoulder compression injury to trapped arm

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 3-5 seconds minimum from lock to tap. Blood chokes can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds.
tap_signals: Physical hand tap (multiple taps on opponent or mat)
Physical foot tap (multiple taps with foot)
Any distress signal or loss of resistance
Immediately release if opponent goes limp
release_protocol: Immediately release arm squeeze and remove head pressure
Step back from opponent's head and shoulders
Allow opponent to breathe and recover (30-60 seconds)
Check for consciousness and normal breathing
If unconscious: position on side, elevate legs, monitor breathing until conscious
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the submission - apply smooth progressive pressure only
Never hold after tap signal - release immediately upon any tap
Always allow tap access - do not trap both arms in training
Never use competition speed in training - practice control first
Stop immediately if opponent's face changes color (purple/red indicates excessive pressure)

variations_and_setups.description: The most common entry where the opponent frames against the choking pressure with their near arm. You swim your choking arm over their frame and behind their neck, trapping their arm against their own carotid while transitioning to head-and-arm control.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent creates a strong near-side frame to defend the shoulder pressure and choking threat

variations_and_setups.description: After establishing the head-and-arm lock, you disengage your hips from the Twister Side Control configuration and walk around to a perpendicular side control angle before applying the final squeeze. This provides maximum chest compression and eliminates space.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: Against larger or more flexible opponents who can create space when you finish from the initial Twister Side Control angle

variations_and_setups.description: From the bottom of a scramble, you sweep the opponent using butterfly hooks while maintaining the head-and-arm grip throughout the transition. You finish the arm triangle from mount or transition to side control for the squeeze.
variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When opponent drives forward and their weight loads onto your hooks

attacker.name: from Twister Side Control Attacker
attacker.description: Step-by-step guide to finishing the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control. Learn grip transitions, finishing angles, and how to capitalize on defensive reactions.
attacker.overview: The Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control attacks the carotid arteries using the opponent's own trapped shoulder combined with your forearm pressure. This finish capitalizes on one of the most common defensive reactions in Twister Side Control: the near-side arm frame against shoulder pressure and lateral torque. When your opponent pushes their arm across to relieve pressure, they inadvertently position their arm against their own neck, creating the head-and-arm configuration. Your task is to recognize this moment, pin the trapped arm with chest pressure, establish the head-and-arm grip, and finish with progressive chest-to-chest compression while controlling the angle. The key advantage of attacking from Twister Side Control is that the rotational torque and leg entanglement already break the opponent's posture and alignment, making the arm triangle finish more accessible than from traditional side control positions.
key_principles: Recognize the frame defense as the trigger to transition to the arm triangle rather than fighting the defense
Maintain constant head control throughout the grip switch to prevent posture recovery during the vulnerable transition moment
Drive the opponent's trapped arm tight against their own neck using chest pressure before attempting the squeeze
Walk your hips perpendicular to the opponent's body toward their trapped-arm side to create the optimal finishing angle
Use progressive chest-to-chest compression rather than arm squeezing to generate the choking pressure
Keep your head low and glued to the mat on the far side of opponent's head to seal the choke and prevent frame escapes
setup_requirements: Established Twister Side Control position with shoulder pressure and controlling grip on opponent's neck
Opponent has created a near-side arm frame across their own neck as a defensive response to the shoulder pressure and choking threat
Your hips are positioned to allow transition from Twister Side Control configuration to perpendicular finishing angle
Sufficient control of opponent's posture to prevent them from standing up or extracting their head during the grip switch
Opponent's trapped arm is loaded against their own carotid with no space between their shoulder and neck

execution_steps.description: From your Twister Side Control top position, feel the opponent push their near-side arm across their own neck to create a frame against your shoulder pressure and choking threat. This arm crossing their neck is your trigger to transition. Do not fight the frame - instead, welcome it as the setup for the arm triangle.

execution_steps.action: Pin the trapped arm with chest pressure
execution_steps.description: Before releasing any part of your controlling grip, drive your chest forward and down onto the opponent's framing arm, pinning it tight against their neck. Your body weight secures the arm in place while you prepare the grip transition. The arm must have no space between their shoulder and their neck.

Release your controlling grip and immediately thread your choking arm over the opponent's trapped arm and behind the back of their neck. Your forearm crosses behind their neck with the blade pressing against the far-side carotid. Move smoothly without creating any gap that would allow head extraction.

execution_steps.action: Lock the figure-four or gable grip
execution_steps.description: Connect your hands by gripping your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind the opponent's head, or use a tight gable grip. The grip must lock the opponent's head and trapped arm together as a unit with no slack in the configuration.

Disengage your legs from the Twister Side Control leg entanglement and walk your hips around toward the opponent's trapped-arm side until you are perpendicular to their body. Your chest should be directly over their face. Each step tightens the choke by removing available space between your bodies.

execution_steps.action: Drop hip and seal the position
execution_steps.description: Drop your hip closest to their trapped arm to the mat, sprawling your weight onto the opponent. Your head drops low to the mat on the far side of their head. This seals the position and removes the space opponents use to breathe or create defensive frames. Your body acts as a wall.

Expand your chest while pulling your elbows together toward your own centerline. The opponent's trapped shoulder compresses one carotid artery while your forearm compresses the other. Apply slow, steady, progressive pressure rather than explosive squeezing. Wait for the tap or feel the resistance fade.

common_counters.counter: Opponent extracts trapped arm before grip is locked
common_counters.your_response: If the arm clears, immediately return to your controlling position in Twister Side Control since the opponent removed their own defense. Reset and wait for the frame to reappear.

common_counters.counter: Opponent bridges and rolls toward the choking arm side
common_counters.your_response: Post your far-side hand and widen your base on the rolling side. If rolled, maintain the grip and finish from bottom using a guard arm triangle configuration.

common_counters.counter: Opponent frames with far arm to create space and prevent chest-to-chest pressure
common_counters.your_response: Use your free hand to strip their far-side frame by swimming inside their elbow. Walk further toward their head to collapse the space their frame creates.

common_counters.counter: Opponent pulls guard and locks closed guard to prevent hip walk-around
common_counters.your_response: Maintain the head-and-arm grip and work to open their guard by posting your knee into their tailbone. Once the guard opens, immediately walk to the finishing angle.

common_errors.error: Releasing controlling grip too early before chest pressure secures the trapped arm
common_errors.consequence: Opponent pulls their arm free during the transition, escaping both the choke setup and the arm triangle attempt, returning to a neutral position
common_errors.correction: Pin the opponent's framing arm with your chest weight before releasing any part of the controlling grip. The arm must be immobilized by body pressure before you initiate the grip switch.

common_errors.error: Squeezing with arms instead of using chest compression and body angle
common_errors.consequence: Arms fatigue rapidly, the choke becomes ineffective, and the opponent can endure the pressure long enough to work an escape or wait for you to gas out
common_errors.correction: Walk to a perpendicular angle and use your dropping hip and expanding chest to generate pressure. Your arms lock the configuration in place while your body creates the compressive force.

common_errors.error: Leaving space between your chest and the opponent's trapped shoulder
common_errors.consequence: The opponent can breathe through the choke and create incremental space to extract their arm or work defensive frames
common_errors.correction: Drop your weight directly onto the opponent's face and trapped shoulder. Your chest must be flush against their body with zero gap. Think about melting your weight through them rather than hovering above.

common_errors.error: Failing to walk hips to perpendicular angle before squeezing
common_errors.consequence: The choke is applied at a suboptimal angle where the opponent's shoulder does not properly compress the carotid, resulting in a neck crank rather than a blood choke
common_errors.correction: Complete the full hip walk-around until you are at a 90-degree angle to the opponent's body. The chest-to-face alignment is what makes the opponent's own shoulder do the choking work.

common_errors.error: Keeping head high instead of dropping it to the mat on the far side
common_errors.consequence: Creates a gap on the far side that the opponent can use to turn their head and relieve pressure, or work their arm free through the space
common_errors.correction: Drop your head to the mat on the far side of the opponent's head immediately after walking to the finishing angle. Your head acts as a seal that prevents the opponent from turning away from the choke.

common_errors.error: Rushing the transition and losing the Twister Side Control position entirely
common_errors.consequence: A sloppy transition gives the opponent time to recover posture, extract their head, and potentially counter to a dominant position
common_errors.correction: The transition should be smooth and deliberate, not explosive. Maintain constant pressure throughout. If the transition stalls, return to your controlling position in Twister Side Control rather than forcing a bad arm triangle.

training_progressions.focus: Developing the smooth switch from controlling grip to head-and-arm configuration
training_progressions.description: Partner starts in Twister Side Control bottom with their near arm across their neck in frame position. Practice the grip switch to arm triangle with zero resistance, focusing on maintaining chest pressure on the trapped arm throughout the transition. Repeat 20 times per side. No finishing attempts.

training_progressions.focus: Walking to the correct angle and generating choke pressure through body mechanics
training_progressions.description: Start with the arm triangle grip already established. Partner gives 30% resistance. Practice walking your hips to the perpendicular angle, dropping your hip, and applying progressive chest compression. Partner provides feedback on pressure location and when the choke becomes effective. Alternate sides.

training_progressions.phase: Phase 3: Transition chain from Twister Side Control
training_progressions.focus: Recognizing the frame defense and flowing to the arm triangle in live motion
training_progressions.description: Partner starts in Twister Side Control bottom and alternates between defending with frames (triggering arm triangle) and defending without frames (staying in position). Practice recognizing which defense is being used and flowing to the appropriate attack. 50% resistance, 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Applying the full technique chain against progressive resistance
training_progressions.description: Start from Twister Side Control top position. Partner gives 70-100% resistance with all defensive options available. Practice the full sequence: recognize frame, transition grip, walk to angle, finish. If the arm triangle fails, return to controlling position and try again. 5-minute rounds with full reset on escape.

flashcards.question: What anatomical structures does the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control attack?
flashcards.answer: The arm triangle compresses both carotid arteries simultaneously. The opponent's own trapped shoulder presses into one carotid from the near side, while your forearm blade crosses behind their neck and presses into the opposite carotid from the far side. This bilateral compression restricts blood flow to the brain, causing unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds if not released.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize when the opponent's defense creates the arm triangle opportunity from Twister Side Control?
flashcards.answer: The trigger is the opponent creating a near-side arm frame across their own neck to relieve shoulder pressure and lateral torque. You will feel their forearm or hand pushing against your choking arm or their own neck. This frame positions their arm exactly where it needs to be for the arm triangle. The moment you feel this defensive frame, begin the transition rather than fighting to maintain the current control.

plausible: They push your choking arm away

flashcards.question: What grip adjustment is required when transitioning from the controlling grip to arm triangle configuration?
flashcards.answer: Release the controlling grip only after chest pressure secures the trapped arm against the opponent's neck. Thread your choking arm over the top of their trapped arm and behind the back of their neck so your forearm blade crosses the far-side carotid. Lock a figure-four grip by grabbing your own bicep with the choking hand while your free hand cups behind their head, or use a gable grip for a tighter configuration.

flashcards.question: Your opponent starts to frame against your shoulder pressure with their near arm - what adjustment capitalizes on this reaction?
flashcards.answer: Drive your chest down onto their framing arm to pin it against their own neck. Once the arm is secured by your body weight, smoothly transition your choking arm over the trapped arm and behind their neck to establish the head-and-arm lock. Do not try to strip the frame - instead, use it as the foundation for the arm triangle. Their defensive action becomes the setup for your next submission.

trap: Pull the frame off their neck

flashcards.question: What body angle creates maximum finishing pressure once the arm triangle is locked from Twister Side Control?
flashcards.answer: Walk your hips until they are perpendicular (90 degrees) to the opponent's body on the trapped-arm side. Drop your near hip to the mat and place your head on the mat on the far side of their head. Your chest should be directly over their face. This angle allows your expanding chest and body weight to drive the opponent's shoulder into their own carotid while your forearm compresses the other side.

flashcards.question: What are the key indicators that the arm triangle is properly locked and the opponent is approaching the point of no escape?
flashcards.answer: The choke is properly locked when you can feel the opponent's trapped shoulder bone pressing firmly into their neck with no space between your chest and their body. Their face will begin changing color as blood flow restricts. Their defensive movements become weaker and less coordinated. If they cannot create any frame with their free hand and cannot bridge effectively, they have passed the point of no escape.

plausible: They still frame with free hand

flashcards.question: What safety precautions must you observe when finishing the arm triangle from Twister Side Control?
flashcards.answer: Apply pressure progressively over 3-5 seconds, never spike or jerk the submission. Monitor the opponent's consciousness by feeling for resistance changes and watching for facial color changes. Always allow at least one hand free for tapping. Release immediately upon any tap signal including verbal, hand, or foot taps. If the opponent goes limp, release immediately and place them in recovery position on their side.
flashcards.answer_line: Apply slow, release on any tap

plausible: Spike it fast for a quick tap
trap: Hold a few seconds after tap

flashcards.question: How do you prevent the opponent from extracting their trapped arm during the transition to the arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: The critical control is chest pressure on the trapped arm before and during the grip switch. Your body weight pins their arm against their own neck so they cannot pull it free. Once the head-and-arm grip is locked, the figure-four configuration mechanically prevents arm extraction. If you feel the arm starting to slide out during transition, immediately return to your controlling position in Twister Side Control rather than chasing a compromised arm triangle.
flashcards.answer_line: Chest pins arm through the switch

plausible: Squeeze biceps to trap the arm
Grab the wrist and yank in
trap: Chase the arm as it slides out

flashcards.question: Your opponent successfully bridges and begins to roll you during the arm triangle attempt - how do you respond?
flashcards.answer: Post your far-side hand immediately and widen your base to absorb the bridge. If the roll succeeds and you end up on bottom, do not release the head-and-arm grip. The arm triangle can be finished from bottom guard position by squeezing your elbows together and using a closed guard to control their posture. The key is maintaining the grip integrity throughout the roll rather than panicking and releasing.
flashcards.answer_line: Post, widen base, keep the grip

plausible: Follow the roll, regrip on top
trap: Let go and scramble to top

flashcards.question: Why is chest compression more effective than arm squeezing for finishing the arm triangle from this position?
flashcards.answer: Chest compression uses your entire body weight and the structural advantage of your torso expanding against the opponent's trapped shoulder and neck. Arm squeezing relies on bicep and forearm endurance, which fatigues rapidly under the sustained effort needed to finish a choke. Body mechanics generate far more compressive force while requiring less energy, and the pressure is distributed across a larger surface area, making the choke tighter and more difficult to defend.

defender.name: from Twister Side Control Defender
defender.description: Learn to defend the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control. Recognize the grip transition, prevent the head-and-arm lock, and escape to safe positions.
defender.overview: Defending the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control requires recognizing the critical transition moment when the attacker shifts from shoulder pressure to head-and-arm control. The primary danger window occurs when you frame against the lateral torque, as this frame can be trapped and used against you. Successful defense demands awareness of arm positioning, immediate reactions to prevent the grip switch, and knowledge of escape timing. Early defense during the transition is far more effective than trying to escape a fully locked arm triangle, so understanding the attacker's sequence is essential for mounting an effective defense. The key defensive insight is that the arm triangle from Twister Side Control requires a specific arm position from you, and controlling where your arm goes is your primary defensive tool.
key_principles: Defend the arm position first - keep your near arm either fully retracted against your body or fully extended away, never crossing your own neck
Recognize the transition moment when the attacker releases their controlling grip as the highest-percentage escape window
Create distance by turning into the attacker rather than away to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
Frame against the attacker's hips and shoulders to prevent them from walking to the finishing angle
If caught, fight the angle by turning toward the attacker to relieve shoulder-on-carotid pressure
Tap early and clearly when the choke is locked - arm triangles restrict blood flow rapidly with minimal warning before unconsciousness
recognition_cues: The attacker drives their chest forward and down onto your framing arm, pinning it against your own neck with unusual deliberateness
The attacker releases their controlling grip and begins threading their arm over your near arm and behind your neck
You feel the attacker's hips disengage from the Twister Side Control leg entanglement and begin walking toward your side
The attacker's head drops low to the mat on the far side of your head as they settle into the finishing position

defensive_options.action: Retract the framing arm before the grip switch completes
defensive_options.when_to_use: During the transition window when the attacker releases their controlling grip to swim over your arm
defensive_options.if_successful: Arm escapes the trap, attacker must return to Twister Side Control top position without the arm triangle setup
defensive_options.risk: If timing is late, you may pull your arm deeper into the trap rather than free it

defensive_options.action: Turn into the attacker and get to knees to prevent the finishing angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker begins walking their hips to the perpendicular angle but has not yet dropped their hip to seal
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing angle and can lead to a scramble back to Twister Side Control position or turtle
defensive_options.risk: Turning incorrectly can expose your back for a back take transition

defensive_options.action: Bridge toward the trapped arm side and pull guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the arm triangle is partially locked but the attacker has not fully sealed the position with their hip and head
defensive_options.if_successful: Creates enough space to pull the attacker into your closed guard where the arm triangle angle is disrupted
defensive_options.risk: A strong bridge against a well-positioned attacker may fail and waste energy

defensive_options.action: Walk feet toward attacker's hips and re-guard
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the attacker has locked the grip but is still adjusting their hip position
defensive_options.if_successful: Disrupts the finishing mechanics by pulling the attacker back into a guard position where they cannot generate chest compression
defensive_options.risk: If the choke is already tight, movement may accelerate the submission

escape_paths: Retract the near arm during the grip transition window and return to defending from Twister Side Control bottom
Turn into the attacker and get to knees to prevent the perpendicular finishing angle
Bridge and shrimp toward the trapped arm side to create space and recover guard
Lock hands together and straighten the trapped arm to prevent the shoulder from compressing the carotid

favorable_outcomes.how: Retract your framing arm during the grip transition, preventing the arm triangle lock. The attacker returns to Twister Side Control top position without the arm triangle, and you resume defending from bottom.

Bridge powerfully toward the trapped arm side while pulling the attacker into your closed guard. The guard position disrupts the finishing angle and removes the chest compression needed to complete the choke.

common_errors.error: Framing across your own neck from Twister Side Control bottom without awareness that this creates the arm triangle setup
common_errors.consequence: Your defensive frame becomes the trapped arm needed for the arm triangle, handing the attacker the submission on a plate
common_errors.correction: When defending from Twister Side Control bottom, keep your near arm either pinned tight to your own body or extended fully away from your neck. Never let your forearm cross your own throat line.

common_errors.error: Turning away from the attacker when caught in the arm triangle
common_errors.consequence: Turning away gives the attacker the perpendicular angle they need and drives your own shoulder deeper into your carotid, accelerating the choke
common_errors.correction: Always turn into the attacker toward the trapped arm side. This flattens the choke angle and prevents your shoulder from compressing your own carotid.

common_errors.error: Waiting too long to defend and trying to escape after the arm triangle is fully locked and sealed
common_errors.consequence: A fully locked arm triangle with the hip dropped and head sealed is extremely difficult to escape. You waste energy fighting a near-certain submission and risk going unconscious.
common_errors.correction: Defend during the transition window when the attacker switches grips. This is when the attacker is most vulnerable. If the arm triangle is fully locked, tap early rather than risking unconsciousness.

common_errors.error: Pushing against the attacker's head instead of their hips when trying to create space
common_errors.consequence: Pushing the head does not disrupt the arm triangle mechanics and wastes arm energy that could be used for more effective escape movements
common_errors.correction: Frame against the attacker's hips and near shoulder to prevent them from walking to the angle. Hip frames disrupt the body mechanics that generate the choke, while head pushes do not.

flashcards.question: How do you recognize that the attacker is transitioning from Twister Side Control to an arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: The key recognition cue is feeling the attacker's chest weight drive down onto your framing arm, pinning it against your own neck, followed by the release of their controlling grip as they begin threading their arm over yours and behind your neck. You may also feel their hips disengage from the Twister Side Control leg entanglement as they prepare to walk to the finishing angle.

plausible: They shift weight to your hips

flashcards.question: What is the safest way to tap when caught in the Arm Triangle from Twister Side Control?
flashcards.answer: Tap immediately and clearly using any available signal: tap the mat or the attacker's body multiple times with your free hand, tap with your feet if hands are trapped, or verbally say 'tap' loudly. Do not wait to see if you can escape once the choke is locked - arm triangles compress the carotid arteries and can cause unconsciousness in 6-8 seconds. Tapping early prevents injury and allows you to continue training.
flashcards.answer_line: Tap early, hands, feet, or voice

plausible: Wait to see if you can escape
Go limp and hope they release
trap: Try to power out before tapping

flashcards.question: What arm positioning prevents the attacker from converting Twister Side Control pressure into an arm triangle?
flashcards.answer: Keep your near arm either pinned tight against your own body with your elbow down and hand on your own chest, or extend it fully away from your neck. The critical mistake is allowing your forearm to cross your own throat line, which creates the trapped-arm position the attacker needs. When defending the shoulder pressure, use head positioning and hip movement rather than arm frames across your neck.
flashcards.answer_line: Never frame arm across own throat

plausible: Post the frame arm on their hip
Push their face with free hand

flashcards.question: The attacker has locked the head-and-arm configuration but has not yet walked to the finishing angle - what escape options remain?
flashcards.answer: This is your last high-percentage escape window. Turn into the attacker toward your trapped-arm side and fight to get to your knees. Simultaneously frame against their hips with your free arm to prevent them from walking to the perpendicular angle. If you can get your knees under you and face into the attacker, they cannot generate the chest compression needed to finish. Alternatively, bridge toward the trapped-arm side and pull them into closed guard.
flashcards.answer_line: Turn in, get to knees, frame hips

plausible: Turtle up and cover your neck
trap: Turn away to hide your neck

flashcards.question: What are the most common defensive errors that allow the arm triangle transition from Twister Side Control?
flashcards.answer: The most common error is instinctively framing across your own neck when defending the shoulder pressure, which directly creates the arm triangle setup. The second most common error is turning away from the attacker once caught, which accelerates the choke by driving your own shoulder into your carotid. The third is waiting too long to defend - the transition window when the attacker switches grips is the best escape opportunity, and it closes within 2-3 seconds.

training_progressions.focus: Identifying the transition cues from Twister Side Control to arm triangle
training_progressions.description: Partner performs the Twister Side Control to arm triangle transition at 25% speed. Practice recognizing each step: chest pressure on frame, grip release, arm swim, grip lock, hip walk. Call out each step as you feel it. No resistance, focus purely on building pattern recognition. 10 repetitions per side.

training_progressions.focus: Retracting the arm during the transition window
training_progressions.description: Partner attempts the grip switch at 50% speed. Practice retracting your arm the moment you feel the controlling grip release. Alternate between successful retractions and intentional failures where partner locks the arm triangle to build escape pattern recognition. 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Turning into the attacker and disrupting the finishing angle when caught
training_progressions.description: Start with the arm triangle already locked but not finished. Partner walks to the angle at 50-70% resistance. Practice turning into the attacker, framing against their hips, and working to recover guard or get to knees. Build the timing for when to bridge versus when to turn in. 3-minute rounds.

training_progressions.focus: Full-speed defense from Twister Side Control position
training_progressions.description: Partner starts in Twister Side Control top with full offensive options. Defend all attacks including the arm triangle transition. Focus on arm positioning awareness to prevent the arm triangle setup while still defending the shoulder pressure. 5-minute rounds, reset on escape or submission.
